title: Chubby: the lock service that became a phone book
dek: In 2006 Mike Burrows described a small service with a big job: give thousands of machines a reliable way to elect a leader and agree on tiny pieces of configuration. Rather than a consensus library, it offered files and locks. It is also one of the most honest papers about how engineers actually use, and misuse, such a service.

items: Chubby is a lock service: a cell of five replicas, kept consistent with Paxos, offering small files and coarse locks that are held for hours or days, not milliseconds.
Its main job is leader election: the server that holds a lock is the primary, and it writes its address into the lock file so everyone can find it.
Locks expire with the holder's session, so a dead primary is replaced within seconds, and sequencers stop an old primary that wakes up late from doing damage.

body.x: The paper: "The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems" by Mike Burrows, OSDI 2006.

GFS and Bigtable each needed exactly one master, and many other systems needed to elect a primary or share a little configuration. Each team could have embedded a Paxos library, but consensus is hard to get right and most teams didn't want to run five machines just to pick a leader. A shared service with a familiar interface, files and locks, was easier to adopt than a library, even for programs not written with distribution in mind.

items: A cell is five replicas. They elect a master with Paxos, and all client requests go to the master; the others copy its database.
Clients open small files and directories, such as /ls/cell/bigtable/master, and can hold a reader or writer lock on any of them.
Each client has a session kept alive by KeepAlive messages. If the session lease, 12 seconds by default, runs out, the client's locks are released.
Clients cache file contents. Before a file changes, the master tells every client caching it to drop its copy, so caches are never stale.
Clients can subscribe to events, such as a file's contents changing or a lock being freed.

body.cap: Electing a primary is just taking a lock. The winner writes its address into the lock file; the others wait for it to be freed, and clients read the file to find whoever currently leads.

body.x: A lock can be lost without its holder knowing: a long garbage-collection pause, a stalled disk or a network partition can outlast the session. The old holder then wakes up still believing it is primary. Chubby's answer is the sequencer, a token naming the lock and its generation number, which the holder attaches to every request it sends. Servers check it and refuse anything older than the newest generation they've seen.

body.cap: The lock alone can't stop a frozen primary from waking up and writing. The generation number can, because the storage server compares it with the newest one it has seen. This pattern is now usually called a fencing token.

items: The biggest use turned out to be naming, not locking: programs read Chubby files to find servers, and that load dwarfed the locks. One cell served about 90,000 clients from a single master.

Developers rarely planned for Chubby being unavailable, so outages of the cell spread to the systems that depended on it. The team added a proxy layer and spent time reviewing how other teams used the service.
Coarse locks, held for long periods, were the right default: they put little load on the cell, and a brief outage barely matters to a lock held for a day.

body.x: ZooKeeper brought the same idea to open source a few years later, and etcd followed. Today leader election in many systems, including Kubernetes controllers, is a lease in one of these stores, with the same session expiry and the same need for fencing tokens.

items: For 'only one worker may run this', such as the payout job in the Job scheduler problem, use a lease in a coordination service such as ZooKeeper or etcd, not a lock row in your main database.
Always add a fencing token: the lock's generation number, checked by whatever the worker writes to. Without it, a paused worker can come back and overwrite the new worker's results.
Use the service for small, slow-changing data: leaders, configuration, membership. Not for the data itself, and not for high-rate locks.
Say what happens when the coordination service is down: the current leader keeps working on its lease for a short grace period, and new elections wait.

body.label: Go deeper: why a service and not a library

body.x: The paper argues that a lock service fits the way programs are actually written. A program usually starts on one machine and grows into a cluster; adding 'take a lock and write your address in a file' is a few lines, while restructuring it around a consensus library is a rewrite. A service also needs only one machine of the client's to be up to make progress, where a library needs a majority of the client's own machines.
